title: A higher COBOL score is not a migrated bank
friendlyTitle: A better COBOL score is not a moved-over bank
summary: The Verge looks at OpenAI's 19 October report on moving old code to newer languages. On OpenAI's tests, GPT-6.1 Sol preserved behavior on 87 percent of COBOL migrations at low reasoning effort and 98 percent at higher effort. A migration counted only if every test passed. OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines told The Verge that legacy code is still far from a solved problem.
friendlySummary: The Verge looks at OpenAI's 19 October report on moving old code into newer languages. On OpenAI's tests, GPT-6.1 Sol kept the original behavior on 87 percent of COBOL moves at a low effort setting, and 98 percent at a higher setting. A move counted only if every test passed. An OpenAI spokesperson, Oscar Haines, told The Verge that old code is still far from a solved problem.
whyItMatters: If your payroll, tax, or card system still runs on COBOL, the number that matters is not a file that compiles. Vadim Zaytsev, who studies software evolution at the University of Twente, told The Verge that rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system, and that the hard part is splitting a live system into pieces that can be swapped one at a time. IBM's figures, cited in the piece, still put COBOL under a large share of banking and cash machines. Those are IBM's numbers. The expert caution is the part you can use: do not schedule a cutover from a benchmark.
